chapter.name: Mechanical Properties of Solids
chapter.blurb: The chapter explains that solids are not perfectly rigid and introduces stress and strain to describe how they deform under stretching, shearing and hydraulic pressure. It states Hooke's law, reads the stress-strain curve of a metal, and defines Young's modulus, the shear modulus, the bulk modulus, Poisson's ratio and the elastic energy stored in a stretched wire. It ends with applications: the thickness of a crane rope, the shape of beams and pillars, and the maximum height of a mountain.

scope_in.item: Distinguish elastic from plastic behaviour and explain that solid bodies are not perfectly rigid
Define stress as restoring force per unit area (F/A), state its unit and dimensional formula, and calculate it, converting cm^2 and mm^2 to m^2

Identify tensile, compressive (longitudinal), shearing (tangential) and hydraulic stress from how the forces are applied, and calculate longitudinal strain Delta L/L, shearing strain Delta x/L = tan theta (about theta) and volume strain Delta V/V
State Hooke's law (stress = k x strain for small deformations) and use the proportionality in the linear region

Describe the stress-strain curve of a metal in words: proportional limit, yield point (elastic limit) and yield strength, permanent set and plastic deformation, ultimate tensile strength, fracture point; classify a material as brittle or ductile; describe elastomers
Define Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(Delta L/L) and use it to find elongation, compression, force, stress or strain for wires, rods and columns, including two wires joined end to end
Interpret a large Young's modulus (steel more elastic than copper, brass and aluminium) using the values of Table 8.1 when given in the question

Define the bulk modulus B = -p/(Delta V/V) and compressibility k = 1/B, explain the negative sign, calculate volume changes under pressure (including pressure h rho g of a liquid column when the formula is given), and compare solids, liquids and gases

concepts.name: Elasticity, stress and strain
concepts.description: Elastic and plastic behaviour, stress as restoring force per unit area, the tensile, compressive, shearing and hydraulic stresses, and the longitudinal, shearing and volume strains.
concepts.idea: A deforming force sets up an equal and opposite restoring force inside a body; the restoring force per unit area is the stress, and the fractional change in dimension it goes with is the strain.
concepts.rule: Elasticity is the property by which a body tends to regain its original size and shape when the applied force is removed; a substance with no such tendency (putty, mud) is plastic. Magnitude of stress = F/A, with SI unit N m^-2 or pascal (Pa) and dimensional formula [M L^-1 T^-2]. Forces normal to the cross-section give tensile stress (stretching) or compressive stress (compression), together called longitudinal stress, and longitudinal strain = Delta L / L. Forces parallel to the cross-section give tangential or shearing stress, and shearing strain = Delta x / L = tan theta, nearly equal to theta for small theta. A fluid pressing normally on the whole surface gives hydraulic stress, equal in magnitude to the hydraulic pressure, and volume strain = Delta V / V, a change of volume with no change of shape. Strain is a ratio and has no unit or dimensional formula.
concepts.example: A force of 800 N normal to a cross-section of 2.0 x 10^-4 m^2 gives a tensile stress of 4.0 x 10^6 N/m^2; a rod 4.0 m long stretched by 1.0 mm has a longitudinal strain of 2.5 x 10^-4.

questions.a: Trial 1: the force is normal to the cross-section, so the stress is tensile. A = 0.10 m x 0.05 m = 5.0 x 10^-3 m^2, stress = 2000 / (5.0 x 10^-3) = 4.0 x 10^5 N/m^2. Ratio = (4.0 x 10^5)/(5.0 x 10^4) = 8. The same force gives very different stresses because the areas over which it acts are different.
s: Trial 1: tensile stress, A = 5.0 x 10^-3 m^2, stress = 4.0 x 10^5 N/m^2
Trial 2: shearing stress, A = 4.0 x 10^-2 m^2, stress = 5.0 x 10^4 N/m^2

s: Judgement - incorrect; solid bodies are not perfectly rigid and even a steel bar can be deformed by a sufficiently large force

questions.q: Using a rectangular block of soft rubber, devise three simple demonstrations, one for each of the three ways in which a solid may change its dimensions under an external force. For each, say how the forces are applied relative to the faces of the block and which ratio you would use as the strain.
questions.a: 1. Longitudinal (tensile or compressive): pull or push on two opposite faces with equal forces normal to those faces; the length changes and the strain is Delta L / L. 2. Shearing: hold the bottom face fixed (for example by gluing it to the table) and push the top face sideways with a force parallel to that face; the top face is displaced by Delta x and the strain is Delta x / L = tan theta, where L is the height of the block. 3. Hydraulic: put the block in a fluid under high pressure so that it is pressed perpendicular to its surface at every point; the volume decreases without change of shape and the strain is Delta V / V.
s: Longitudinal case: equal forces normal to opposite faces, strain = Delta L / L
Shearing case: equal and opposite forces parallel to opposite faces (one face held), strain = Delta x / L (= tan theta)
Hydraulic case: fluid pressure normal to the surface everywhere, strain = Delta V / V

concepts.name: Hooke's law and the stress-strain curve
concepts.description: Hooke's law for small deformations and the regions and points of the stress-strain curve of a metal: proportional limit, yield point, permanent set, ultimate tensile strength and fracture; brittle and ductile materials and elastomers.
concepts.idea: For small deformations stress is proportional to strain, but the full stress-strain curve of a metal shows where this stops, where the deformation becomes permanent and where the material breaks.
concepts.rule: Hooke's law: stress = k x strain, where k is the modulus of elasticity; it is an empirical law valid for most materials. On the curve for a metal (Fig. 8.2): from O to A the curve is linear and Hooke's law is obeyed (A is the proportional limit); from A to B stress and strain are not proportional but the body still returns to its original dimension; B is the yield point or elastic limit and its stress is the yield strength sigma_y. Beyond B the strain increases rapidly even for a small change in stress, and on unloading from a point C between B and D the strain does not return to zero: the material has a permanent set and the deformation is plastic. D marks the ultimate tensile strength sigma_u; beyond D additional strain is produced even by a reduced force and fracture occurs at E. If D and E are close the material is brittle; if far apart it is ductile. Elastomers such as rubber and the tissue of the aorta have a very large elastic region but do not obey Hooke's law over most of it and have no well defined plastic region.
concepts.example: If a stress of 2 x 10^7 N/m^2 produces a strain of 1.6 x 10^-4 in the proportional region, a stress of 7 x 10^7 N/m^2 produces a strain of 5.6 x 10^-4.

questions.q: A test wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 x 10^-6 m^2 is stretched by a force that is increased in steps. The stress-strain graph is a straight line up to a force of 360 N. The wire returns to its original length for every force up to 400 N, but not beyond. The largest force the wire sustains is 700 N, after which it breaks at a smaller force. questions.a: Stress = force / area. Proportional limit (end of the straight-line part): 360 N / (2.0 x 10^-6 m^2) = 1.8 x 10^8 N/m^2. Yield strength (stress at the yield point or elastic limit, the largest stress from which the wire still recovers): 400 / (2.0 x 10^-6) = 2.0 x 10^8 N/m^2. Ultimate tensile strength (the largest stress on the curve): 700 / (2.0 x 10^-6) = 3.5 x 10^8 N/m^2.
s: Stress at the proportional limit = 360/(2.0 x 10^-6) = 1.8 x 10^8 N/m^2, identified as the end of the linear part
Yield strength = 400/(2.0 x 10^-6) = 2.0 x 10^8 N/m^2, identified with the elastic limit
Ultimate tensile strength = 700/(2.0 x 10^-6) = 3.5 x 10^8 N/m^2, identified with the largest force

questions.q: A wire has a proportional limit of 1.8 x 10^8 N/m^2, and in its proportional region stress = (2.0 x 10^11 N/m^2) x strain. A student uses this relation to predict the strain at a stress of 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2 and gets 1.5 x 10^-3. Explain why this prediction cannot be trusted, and state whether the actual strain is larger or smaller than the predicted value.
questions.a: Hooke's law (stress proportional to strain) holds only in the linear part of the curve, up to the proportional limit of 1.8 x 10^8 N/m^2. A stress of 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2 is beyond this, where the curve is no longer a straight line and the strain increases more rapidly with stress. So the actual strain is larger than the predicted 1.5 x 10^-3.
s: States that the linear relation is valid only up to the proportional limit, and 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2 lies beyond it
Concludes the actual strain is larger than predicted, because beyond the linear region strain rises faster with stress

questions.q: A metal wire of original length 2.0 m is tested to destruction. At its proportional limit the strain is 0.0010, and at fracture the strain is 0.25. Find the extension of the wire (a) at the proportional limit and (b) at fracture, and (c) compare the two and say what the comparison shows about where most of the stretching of this wire takes place.
questions.a: (a) Extension = strain x original length = 0.0010 x 2.0 m = 2.0 x 10^-3 m = 2.0 mm. (b) Extension at fracture = 0.25 x 2.0 m = 0.50 m. (c) The extension at fracture is 0.50 / 0.0020 = 250 times the extension at the proportional limit. So only a very small part of the total stretching happens in the linear region where Hooke's law holds; almost all of it happens afterwards, where the deformation is plastic.
s: Extension at the proportional limit = 0.0010 x 2.0 m = 2.0 mm
Extension at fracture = 0.25 x 2.0 m = 0.50 m
Ratio 250, and the conclusion that nearly all the stretching occurs beyond the linear (Hooke's law) region, as plastic deformation

questions.a: The statement is not correct. Returning to the original shape shows that rubber has a very large elastic region, but obeying Hooke's law means that stress is proportional to strain. Rubber is an elastomer: its stress-strain curve is not a straight line and it does not obey Hooke's law over most of its elastic region, whereas a metal such as steel does obey it in its (small) proportional region.
s: Judgement - incorrect; regaining shape (being elastic) is not the same as stress being proportional to strain
States that rubber is an elastomer which does not obey Hooke's law over most of its elastic region

concepts.name: Young's modulus
concepts.description: Young's modulus as the ratio of tensile or compressive stress to longitudinal strain, its use to find elongation, force or strain in wires, rods and columns, and what a large Young's modulus means.
concepts.idea: Young's modulus measures how hard it is to change the length of a material: the larger it is, the larger the force needed for a given small change in length.
concepts.rule: Y = (tensile or compressive stress)/(longitudinal strain) = (F/A)/(Delta L/L) = F L/(A Delta L). The strain produced is the same whether the stress is tensile or compressive. Strain is dimensionless, so the unit of Y is that of stress, N m^-2 or Pa. Y is a characteristic of the material. Metals have large Young's moduli, so a large force is needed for a small change in length; steel needs a larger force than copper, brass or aluminium for the same strain and is therefore more elastic. Wood, bone, concrete and glass have rather small Young's moduli.
concepts.example: A copper wire (Y = 1.1 x 10^11 N/m^2) of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 4.0 x 10^-6 m^2 pulled by 220 N stretches by Delta L = F L/(A Y) = (220 x 2.0)/(4.0 x 10^-6 x 1.1 x 10^11) = 1.0 x 10^-3 m = 1.0 mm.

concepts.name: Shear modulus, bulk modulus and compressibility
concepts.description: The shear modulus (modulus of rigidity) for a shearing stress, the bulk modulus for a hydraulic stress, compressibility as its reciprocal, and how these moduli compare for solids, liquids and gases.
concepts.idea: A shear modulus tells how hard it is to change the shape of a solid, and a bulk modulus how hard it is to change the volume of a solid, liquid or gas.
concepts.rule: Shear modulus G = (shearing stress)/(shearing strain) = (F/A)/(Delta x/L) = F L/(A Delta x) = F/(A theta), so the shearing stress = G x theta. G is generally less than Y; for most materials G is about Y/3. Bulk modulus B = -p/(Delta V/V); the negative sign shows that an increase in pressure produces a decrease in volume, so B is always positive. The unit of G and B is N m^-2 or Pa. Compressibility k = 1/B = -(1/Delta p) x (Delta V/V), the fractional change in volume per unit increase in pressure. Bulk moduli of solids are much larger than those of liquids, which are much larger than those of gases; gases are about a million times more compressible than solids. Shear changes shape but not volume and is possible only in solids; hydraulic stress changes volume but not shape and applies to solids, liquids and gases.
concepts.example: A shearing stress of 4.2 x 10^7 N/m^2 on copper (G = 4.2 x 10^10 N/m^2) gives a shearing strain of 1.0 x 10^-3; a pressure increase of 1.4 x 10^8 N/m^2 on copper (B = 1.4 x 10^11 N/m^2) gives a volume strain of magnitude 1.0 x 10^-3.

concepts.name: Poisson's ratio and elastic potential energy in a stretched wire
concepts.description: Lateral strain and Poisson's ratio for a stretched wire, and the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched wire and per unit volume.
concepts.idea: A stretched wire also becomes thinner, by a fixed fraction of its longitudinal strain, and the work done in stretching it is stored in it as elastic potential energy.
concepts.rule: The strain perpendicular to the applied force is the lateral strain, Delta d/d. Within the elastic limit it is directly proportional to the longitudinal strain, and Poisson's ratio = (lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain) = (Delta d/d)/(Delta L/L) = (Delta d/Delta L) x (L/d). It is a pure number with no dimensions or units, and depends only on the nature of the material (0.28 to 0.30 for steels, about 0.33 for aluminium alloys). For a wire of length L and area A stretched by l, the force is F = Y A l/L, and the work done, stored as elastic potential energy, is W = (1/2)(Y A/L) l^2 = (1/2) x Young's modulus x strain^2 x volume = (1/2) x stress x strain x volume. The elastic potential energy per unit volume is u = (1/2) x sigma x epsilon.
concepts.example: A wire of diameter 2.5 mm contracts by 0.00175 mm in diameter when its longitudinal strain is 0.0025: lateral strain = 0.0007 and Poisson's ratio = 0.28. If a wire is under a stress of 8.0 x 10^7 N/m^2 at a strain of 4.0 x 10^-4, the energy stored per unit volume is (1/2) x 8.0 x 10^7 x 4.0 x 10^-4 = 1.6 x 10^4 J/m^3.

concepts.name: Applications of the elastic behaviour of materials
concepts.description: Choosing the thickness of a crane rope from the yield strength, the sag of a loaded beam and the I-shaped section, the shape of pillars, and the estimate of the maximum height of a mountain.
concepts.idea: Engineering designs keep the stress in a material below its elastic limit and choose shapes that limit bending for the least material; the same idea limits how high a mountain can be.
concepts.rule: Crane rope: the extension must not exceed the elastic limit, so the area of cross-section must satisfy A >= W/sigma_y = M g/sigma_y; a margin of safety of about a factor of ten in the load is added, and ropes are made of many thin wires braided together for ease in manufacture, flexibility and strength. Beam: a bar of length l, breadth b and depth d loaded at the centre by W and supported near its ends sags by delta = W l^3/(4 b d^3 Y); a large Y and a short span reduce the sag, and increasing the depth is more effective than increasing the breadth, but a deep thin bar may buckle, so the I-shaped section is used: a large load-bearing surface and enough depth, with less weight and cost. A pillar with rounded ends supports less load than one with a distributed shape at the ends. Mountain: the base is not under uniform compression; its sides are free, so there is a shear component of stress of about h rho g, and the greatest possible height is the h at which h rho g reaches the elastic limit (critical shearing stress) of rock, beyond which the rock at the base would flow.
concepts.example: A rope that must carry 9000 N in a steel of yield strength 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2 needs A >= 9000/(3.0 x 10^8) = 3.0 x 10^-5 m^2. Tripling the depth of a centrally loaded beam reduces its sag to 1/27.

questions.q: On a certain planet g = 4.0 m/s^2. The rock there has density 2.5 x 10^3 kg/m^3 and an elastic limit of 2.0 x 10^8 N/m^2. Using the chapter's estimate that the stress at the base of a mountain of height h is about h rho g, find the maximum height of a mountain on this planet.
questions.a: At the maximum height the stress at the base equals the elastic limit of the rock: h rho g = 2.0 x 10^8 N/m^2. So h = (2.0 x 10^8)/(2.5 x 10^3 kg/m^3 x 4.0 m/s^2) = (2.0 x 10^8)/(1.0 x 10^4) = 2.0 x 10^4 m = 20 km.
s: Equates h rho g to the elastic limit of the rock

questions.q: A crane is to lift a load of mass 3000 kg. The steel of its rope has a yield strength of 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2, and a safety factor of 10 in the load is to be provided. Take g = 10 m/s^2. The cross-sectional area of rope required is

A steel bar of length 2.0 m, breadth 0.020 m and depth 0.050 m is supported near its ends and loaded at the centre. For such a bar the sag is delta = W l^3/(4 b d^3 Y). Take Young's modulus of steel = 2.0 x 10^11 N/m^2. Find (a) the sag for a central load of 1000 N, and (b) the central load for which the sag would be only 1.0 mm.
questions.a: (a) l^3 = 8.0 m^3 and d^3 = (0.050)^3 = 1.25 x 10^-4 m^3. delta = (1000 x 8.0)/(4 x 0.020 x 1.25 x 10^-4 x 2.0 x 10^11) = 8000/(2.0 x 10^6) = 4.0 x 10^-3 m = 4.0 mm. (b) For a given bar the sag is proportional to the load, so for 1.0 mm the load is 1000 N x (1.0/4.0) = 250 N.
s: Substitutes correctly, with l^3 = 8.0 m^3 and d^3 = 1.25 x 10^-4 m^3
W = 250 N for a sag of 1.0 mm, by proportionality (delta proportional to W) or by direct substitution in the formula

questions.a: Only II

questions.q: For a crane rope the minimum radius works out to about 1 cm, yet after allowing a safety factor of ten in the load a radius of only about 3 cm is recommended, not 10 cm. Explain why, taking sqrt(10) = 3.2.
questions.a: The required area of cross-section is A = (load)/(yield strength), so it is proportional to the load: ten times the load needs ten times the area. For a circular rope A = pi r^2, so the radius is proportional to sqrt(A) and increases by a factor of sqrt(10) = 3.2 only. Hence the radius goes from about 1 cm to about 3 cm.
s: States that the area is proportional to the load, so the area must be ten times larger
Uses A = pi r^2 to show the radius increases by sqrt(10) = 3.2, i.e. to about 3 cm

questions.q: A bar of length l, breadth b and depth d, made of a material of Young's modulus Y, is supported near its ends and loaded at the centre by a load W. It sags by delta = W l^3/(4 b d^3 Y). Bar P has breadth 4 cm and depth 2 cm; bar Q has breadth 2 cm and depth 4 cm. They are of the same material and length, so they contain the same amount of material, and they carry the same central load. Compare their sags, and explain why the depth of a bar cannot simply be increased more and more to reduce the sag.
questions.a: The sag is proportional to 1/(b d^3). For P, b d^3 = 4 x 2^3 = 32 cm^4; for Q, b d^3 = 2 x 4^3 = 128 cm^4. So sag of Q / sag of P = 32/128 = 1/4: Q sags only one quarter as much as P with the same amount of material. However, a deep and thin bar may bend sideways (buckle) unless the load is exactly at the right place, which is why depth cannot be increased without limit and the I-shaped section is used as a compromise.
s: Uses delta proportional to 1/(b d^3) for both bars, in any form (b d^3 = 32 cm^4 for P and 128 cm^4 for Q, or breadth factor 2 and depth factor 1/8)
Sag of Q = 1/4 of the sag of P
Explains the limit: a deep thin bar may buckle unless the load is exactly at the right place

questions.q: A student argues that, because rock is very strong, a mountain 100 km high could exist on earth. Take the density of rock = 3.0 x 10^3 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2 and the elastic limit of a typical rock = 3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2, and use the chapter's estimate that the stress at the base of a mountain of height h is about h rho g. Evaluate the argument.
questions.a: The argument fails. For h = 100 km = 1.0 x 10^5 m, h rho g = 1.0 x 10^5 x 3.0 x 10^3 x 10 = 3.0 x 10^9 N/m^2, which is ten times the elastic limit of rock (3.0 x 10^8 N/m^2), so the rock at the base would flow. The stress stays within the elastic limit only up to h = (3.0 x 10^8)/(3.0 x 10^3 x 10) = 1.0 x 10^4 m = 10 km.
s: Calculates h rho g = 3.0 x 10^9 N/m^2 for 100 km and shows it exceeds the elastic limit, so the rock would flow
Gives the limiting height: h = 1.0 x 10^4 m = 10 km

questions.q: Design the steel rope for a lift whose total mass, with passengers, is 2000 kg. The steel has a yield strength of 2.5 x 10^8 N/m^2 and a safety factor of 10 in the load is required. The rope is to be braided from thin wires, each of cross-sectional area 2.0 x 10^-6 m^2. Take g = 10 m/s^2. Find the total cross-sectional area needed and the number of wires, and state the tensile stress in the rope when it carries the actual load.
questions.a: Actual load = Mg = 2000 x 10 = 2.0 x 10^4 N; design load = 10 x 2.0 x 10^4 = 2.0 x 10^5 N. Area needed A = design load / yield strength = (2.0 x 10^5)/(2.5 x 10^8) = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^2. Number of wires = (8.0 x 10^-4)/(2.0 x 10^-6) = 400. With the actual load the stress is (2.0 x 10^4)/(8.0 x 10^-4) = 2.5 x 10^7 N/m^2, one-tenth of the yield strength, so the rope stays well within its elastic limit.
s: Design load = 2.0 x 10^5 N and area = design load / yield strength = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^2
Number of wires = 400
Stress at the actual load = 2.5 x 10^7 N/m^2, one-tenth of the yield strength (within the elastic limit)
